stances.claim: Traditionally and by default, habeas corpus 'has only one objective: to inquire into the cause of the detention' - and the writ will NOT issue when detention is made pursuant to a lawful court order with jurisdiction, especially in capital-offense cases.

Reyes v. Director (January 17, 2023) nonetheless issued the writ freeing Gigi Reyes from Taguig City Jail despite her detention pursuant to a Sandiganbayan plunder order - as an exception, because her custody had become 'vexatious, capricious, and oppressive, amounting to an infringement on the constitutional right to speedy trial' - but conditioned release on four obligations.
stances.rhetorical_move: exception-doctrine identification with four-condition release-modality summary

stances.claim: The Court's exception deviates from settled doctrine in FIVE distinct ways: no bond; contrary to settled jurisprudence that release should be unconditional and absolute (accused 'acquitted pronto'); contrary to Sec 4 Rule 102 (custody under valid process bars the writ - >P172M plunder charges validated her detention); contrary to constitutional rule that capital-offense detainees release only if evidence 'not strong'; contrary to rule that habeas corpus is unavailable when bail has been denied.
Additionally, the release order appears to deprive prosecutors and government of due process - not impleaded, not notified, denied chance to oppose - yet ruled to have violated speedy trial.

The release order also contradicts the IRSC because it was issued as an 'unsigned resolution' (UR) signed only by the Division Clerk of Court - lacking IRSC-required member signatures, Division Chairman attestation, and Chief Justice certification - and under the IRSC a UR disposing of a case on the merits is 'essentially meaningful only to the parties,' has no doctrinal value, does not constitute precedent, and binds only the parties.
SolGen Menardo I. Guevarra and team filed on February 3 a 'little-known but... formidable' Omnibus Motion attacking the UR - on which the Court has not acted as of column date.

Despite the well-reasoned OM, the Gigi exception - IMHO - should be applied (unless reversed or modified) in the spirit of fairness to future cases on all fours and in pari materia, where the petitioner can match the eight-element Gigi fact pattern.
Open questions: How will the Court decide the SolGen's OM? Will Leila de Lima's planned habeas corpus petition succeed despite her bail denial? Abangan!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the doctrine of habeas corpus - traditionally, an order directing a person detaining another to produce the physical body and explain the reason, with the single objective of inquiring into the cause of detention; the writ will NOT issue when detention is pursuant to a lawful court order with jurisdiction, especially in capital-offense cases. In Reyes v. Director (January 17, 2023), however, the Supreme Court's First Division issued the writ freeing Jessica Lucila 'Gigi' Reyes from Taguig City Jail despite her detention pursuant to a Sandiganbayan plunder order - as an exception, because her custody had become 'vexatious, capricious, and oppressive, amounting to an infringement on the constitutional right to speedy trial' - releasing her on four conditions (personal hearing attendance, quarterly whereabouts reports to the SBN, SBN-travel authority with 5-day return report, and quarterly SC compliance reports). Panganiban itemizes FIVE distinct doctrinal deviations: no bond required; contrary to settled jurisprudence that release should be unconditional and absolute (accused 'acquitted pronto'); contrary to Section 4 Rule 102 (custody under valid process bars the writ - and the >P172 million plunder charges validated her detention); contrary to the constitutional rule that capital-offense detainees may be released only if prosecution evidence is 'not strong'; and contrary to the rule that habeas corpus is unavailable when bail has already been denied. He also notes that the release order appears to deprive prosecutors of due process - not impleaded, not notified, denied any chance to oppose - yet ruled to have violated speedy trial. Moreover, the order contradicts the IRSC because it was issued as an 'unsigned resolution' signed only by the Division Clerk of Court, lacking required member signatures, Division Chairman attestation, and Chief Justice certification - and under the IRSC, a UR disposing of a case on the merits is 'essentially meaningful only to the parties,' has no doctrinal value, does not constitute precedent, and binds only the parties. Solicitor General Menardo I. Guevarra and team filed on February 3 a 'little-known but... formidable' Omnibus Motion of the UR, which the Court has not acted on. Despite the well-reasoned OM, Panganiban argues that in the spirit of fairness the Gigi exception should be applied (unless reversed or modified) to future cases on all fours and in pari materia - matching the eight-element Gigi pattern (~9-year detention; trial commencing only March 3, 2022; Information filed June 5, 2014; delays from wrong markings of evidence; two confusing SBN pretrial orders; one-witness-per-day limit despite twice-weekly schedule; thousands of exhibits; no prosecution explanation for the long-drawn-out proceedings). He closes with two open questions: how will the Court decide the SolGen's OM, and will Leila de Lima's planned habeas corpus petition succeed despite her bail denial? Abangan!
